prime.problem: When arrivals exceed capacity, an unbounded queue keeps the server 100% busy while every answer it produces is late. And the usual dashboards hide it: the mean latency looks healthy while the tail blows the SLO, and "up 99.9% of the time" says nothing about how many requests were lost at peak.
prime.fits: Builds on the sizing card's queue model (a busy core, 10 conversions/s) and the partial-failure card's timeouts. It gives the course its measuring sticks: p99 instead of mean, yield instead of uptime, harvest for partial answers.
expect: backpressure: a bounded queue that rejects fast
harvest: answer with less, or refuse
prime.goal: Show with numbers why a capped queue beats an unbounded one under overload, why fan-out turns one server's p99 into everyone's median, and choose between lower yield and lower harvest for a given query.

attend: With 12/s into a core that does 10, after how many seconds is every finished image already late, and why does a cap of 4 stop that?
Why is the mean (81 ms) nowhere near the p99 (475 ms) in the lognormal sample?
What does fan-out to 100 servers do to a 1% slow rate, and why is one server's p99 now the system's median?
Why do two 60-second outages with identical uptime have different yields?
When shard B is down, when is answering from A and C the wrong choice?

must: Arrivals 12/s > service 10/s → an unbounded backlog grows 2/s → wait = backlog / 10 → after 2 s every image finishes late, while the core stays 100% busy → cap the queue at 4 so the extra 2/s get an immediate error and back off (latency ≤ 0.5 s for the 83.3% served)
Latency has a long right tail → the mean is pulled up by the tail but lands far below it (81 ms vs p99 475 ms) → judge a service by its percentiles, because users in the tail are the ones who leave
A request waits for n parallel calls → it is as slow as the slowest → P(slow) = 1 − (1 − p)<sup>n</sup> → 1% slow per server becomes 63.4% of requests at n = 100
Uptime counts seconds, yield counts requests → the same 60 s outage costs 60,000 requests at the trough and 600,000 at peak → yield 99.987% vs 99.874%: one meets 99.9%, the other misses
elevated: Median of the max of 100 draws = the 100·0.51/100 ≈ 99.31st percentile → with fan-out 100 the typical request sees one server's p99.31 (542 ms) → tail-tolerant tricks (hedged requests, fewer fan-out calls) matter more than speeding up the median
reference: the lognormal parameters (median 50 ms, σ = 1.0, seed 7)
Fox and Brewer / Dean and Barroso citations

compress.prompt: From memory, write four short chains: overload → backpressure; tail → percentiles; fan-out → tail amplification; outage → yield vs uptime. Put one number from the card on each.
checklist: unbounded queue: 12 s wait after 60 s; capped: ≤ 0.5 s, 16.7% rejected
harvest 67% with shard B down, or refuse and keep harvest 100%
reject fast, retry with backoff: overload becomes a signal, not a queue

retrieve.q: Explain why an unbounded queue under a 20% surge is worse than rejecting 2 requests in 12, even though the unbounded one "loses nothing".
answer: every request is eventually served, but after 2 s every one is served late (wait > 0.4 s)
the core spends its time on images nobody is waiting for any more
with a cap, 10 of 12 finish within 0.5 s and the other 2 learn at once and can back off

retrieve.q: Walk through queue(12, 10, 60, cap=4) for the first three seconds: backlog, wait and rejections each tick.
answer: t = 1: 12 in, room 14, all taken; backlog 2, wait 0.2 s, 0 rejected
t = 2: room 12, all taken; backlog 4, wait 0.4 s, 0 rejected
t = 3: room 10 + 4 − 4 = 10; 2 rejected; backlog stays 4, wait 0.4 s
from then on 2/s are rejected: 116 by t = 60

retrieve.q: A search over 3 shards has shard B down. For a product search and for a billing total, choose lower harvest or lower yield and justify each.
answer: product search: answer from A and C (harvest 67%); a partial list is still useful
billing total: refuse (yield drops, harvest stays 100%); a sum over 2 of 3 shards is a wrong answer
the rule: lower harvest only when a partial answer isn't a wrong answer

retrieve.q: Why is the mean still the right number for capacity planning, even on a card that argues against it?
answer: total CPU used is mean × count, so the 1K-core sizing is mean-based
percentiles are for latency promises; means are for resource totals
and a p99 from 100 samples is just the second-slowest request: you need data to trust it

compare.q: Backpressure says "reject fast and let callers back off"; the retries card says how to back off. What goes wrong if backpressure is paired with instant retries, and which two mechanisms from that card fix it?
answer: rejected callers retry at once: the core that could do 10/s is offered 24/s (the card's cascade)
full-jitter exponential backoff spreads the retries out in time
retrying at one layer only stops (r + 1)<sup>L</sup> amplification

compare.q: cs-4 uses expected values to size things; this card says the mean lies about latency. What's the precise difference in what each summary answers?
answer: the expected value answers "how much in total" (CPU, bytes, cost)
a percentile answers "how bad for the unlucky users"
skewed distributions separate them: mean 81 ms, p99 475 ms in the same sample

predict.q: The surge doubles: 20 requests/s into the same core, still capped at 4 waiting. What fraction is answered, what is the worst latency of an answered request, and how does the answered fraction compare with the 12/s case? Commit first.
predict.answer: The core still serves 10/s and the cap still bounds the wait at 0.4 s, so answered requests still finish within 0.5 s. But now 10 of 20 are rejected each second: yield falls to 50% (from 83.3%). Backpressure protects latency, never throughput: past capacity, every extra request becomes a rejection. That's the signal to add cores, not to raise the cap.

apply.task: Run queue() from code/backpressure-metrics.py for a 50% surge (15/s into 10/s) for 10 s, unbounded and with cap = 4. Then use p_slow to find what fraction of requests are slow for fan-out 10 with the sample's per-call rate p = 0.9%, and for fan-out 20 with p = 1%.
apply.done: You get (10, 50, 5.0, 0) unbounded and (10, 4, 0.4, 46) capped, an answered share of 10/15 = 66.7%, and fan-out results of 8.6% and 18.2%.
apply.hint: Unbounded backlog = (15 − 10) × 10 = 50, wait 50 / 10 = 5.0 s. Capped: 5 rejected per second from t = 2 on, plus 1 in the tick the queue fills: 46. 1 − 0.991<sup>10</sup> = 0.0864; 1 − 0.99<sup>20</sup> = 0.1821.
